## People hub: schema and permission model

Design doc for the Directus data model behind Layer 2 of `docs/architecture.md` (the CRM / people
hub), per the plan agreed on issue #69. Covers the collections, fields, and permission policies;
deployment and rollout are tracked in the sibling issues (#92-#95) that decompose #69.

### Scope and non-goals

- Models what Clubspot actually gives us: people, their guardian/emergency-contact relationships,
  programs/sessions, and registrations. No household grouping — Clubspot has no concept of a
  household, only per-registration guardians and emergency contacts, so that's what the schema keys
  off.
- Terminology matches Clubspot and the website: **program** (Clubspot's `Camp`), **session**
  (`CampSession`), **registration** (`Registration`) — not "enrollment." Clubspot's **class**
  (`CampClass`) concept is named for, but not modeled by, this schema — see the `programs`/`sessions`
  note below.
- Auth identity is deliberately separate from person data — see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)
  below.
- Coach and guardian **portals** (thin clients calling this API) are out of scope; this doc defines
  the roles/policies they'll eventually use, but nothing here provisions their logins. That's #65.

### Collections

**people** — one row per human known to the org: staff, coaches, guardians, participants, emergency
contacts. Roles aren't stored — they're derived from relationships: staff from `directus_user_id` +
Directus role, coach from an `event_staff` row, guardian/emergency contact from a `contacts` row,
participant from a `registrations` row.

No `clubspot_id` here. Clubspot has no stable person record — each registration carries its own
contact data, and one real person can show up as the contact on many registrations. Deduplicating
and collecting those into a single `people` row (by email, most likely) is the identity-resolution
problem #70's sync has to solve; it isn't a field this schema can just copy in.

| Field                     | Type                                              | Notes                               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `id`                      | uuid                                              | primary key                         |
| `first_name`, `last_name` | string                                            |                                     |
| `email`, `phone`          | string, nullable                                  | contact info, not auth              |
| `date_of_birth`           | date, nullable                                    | required for minors                 |
| `directus_user_id`        | uuid, nullable, unique, FK -> `directus_users.id` | see [Auth identity](#auth-identity) |

**medical_profiles** — one-to-one with `people`, kept as its own collection so its permission policy
can be stricter than a roster-level `people` read (allergies, medications, conditions, physician
contact).

| Field                                    | Type                        | Notes                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `person_id`                              | uuid, PK, FK -> `people.id` | one profile per person, so `person_id` is the key |
| `allergies`, `medications`, `conditions` | text                        | free-form                                         |
| `physician_name`, `physician_phone`      | string, nullable            |                                                   |

**contacts** — one join collection for both relationship kinds Clubspot gives us (guardian and
emergency contact), rather than a separate table per type, since the shape is identical. Other
relationship kinds, if they're ever needed, get their own dedicated table rather than growing this
one's `relationship_type` enum.

Like `people`, these rows have no Clubspot id of their own to key off — Clubspot doesn't model a
guardian/emergency contact as a linked record, just flat strings on the participant
(`parentGuardianName`/`_secondary`, `emergencyContact`/`emergencyRelationship`). `contact_order`
is what recovers Clubspot's primary-vs-secondary guardian distinction once #70 turns those flat
fields into rows here.

| Field               | Type                                   | Notes                                     |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `id`                | uuid                                   | primary key                               |
| `related_person_id` | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the minor                                 |
| `person_id`         | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the guardian or emergency contact         |
| `relationship_type` | enum (`guardian`, `emergency_contact`) |                                           |
| `contact_order`     | integer                                | call order when a minor has more than one |

**event_staff** — coach/staff assigned to a session. This is the row that makes someone a "coach"
(derived, not stored on `people`) — not used to scope roster permissions yet, see
[Permission model](#permission-model).

| Field        | Type                      | Notes       |
| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----------- |
| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
| `person_id`  | uuid, FK -> `people.id`   |             |
| `session_id` | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id` |             |

**programs** — matches org/Clubspot terminology: a program is what CYC calls a `Camp` in Clubspot
(e.g. "Youth Camp", "LTS Weekday", "ILCA Race Team") — the thing on the website you sign up for.

| Field              | Type                     | Notes                                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                | uuid                     | primary key                                    |
| `name`              | string                   |                                                 |
| `category`          | string, nullable         | Clubspot's own grouping (e.g. "Summer Camp", "Junior Racing", "Adult Sailing") |
| `clubspot_camp_id`  | string, nullable, unique | dedup key for #70                              |

**sessions** — a dated instance of a program (Clubspot's `CampSession`).

| Field                    | Type                      | Notes             |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `id`                     | uuid                      | primary key       |
| `program_id`             | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` |                   |
| `start_date`, `end_date` | date                      |                   |
| `clubspot_session_id`    | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70 |

**classes** — an age/skill subdivision within a program (Clubspot's `CampClass`, e.g. "Beginner" vs.
"Advanced"). Modeled now, not deferred: a registration is for a specific session *and* class, and
#70's sync needs somewhere to put that — see `registrations` below.

| Field                | Type                      | Notes             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `id`                  | uuid                      | primary key       |
| `program_id`          | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` | a class belongs to the program, independent of which sessions offer it |
| `name`                | string                   |                   |
| `clubspot_class_id`   | string, nullable, unique | dedup key for #70 |

Not modeled: which classes a given session offers (Clubspot's `CampSession.campClassesArray`) or
per-class/session capacity (`EntryCap`) — that's capacity-planning territory for the
financial-model-replacement app, not something the people hub's roster/permission needs require.

**registrations** — a participant's registration for one session + class (Clubspot's own term —
matched here rather than "enrollment"). This is deliberately at Clubspot's finest grain, its
`RegistrationCampSession` join ("Session Join Id" in the existing `ParticipantsReport`) rather than
its parent `Registration` object: a single Clubspot registration spanning multiple weeks/classes
becomes multiple rows here, one per session+class, matching what the current spreadsheet already
does. Billing/payment (Clubspot's `billing_registration`) stays out of scope, same as the rest of
the financial model.

| Field                       | Type                                        | Notes                                                       |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                        | uuid                                        | primary key                                                 |
| `person_id`                 | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                     | the participant                                             |
| `session_id`                | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id`                   |                                                              |
| `class_id`                  | uuid, FK -> `classes.id`                    |                                                              |
| `status`                    | enum (`confirmed`, `waitlist`, `cancelled`) | same vocabulary as #60; the *current* status — see [Change tracking](#change-tracking) for history |
| `clubspot_registration_id`  | string, nullable                            | groups rows from the same parent Clubspot registration (a multi-session signup); **not unique alone** |
| `clubspot_session_join_id`  | string, nullable, unique                    | the true per-row dedup key for #70 (`RegistrationCampSession`'s own id) |

### Change tracking

Registration status isn't a fact that just happens once — a row moves waitlist → confirmed →
cancelled, and knowing *when* matters (for reporting, and because Clubspot itself already tracks
it: `RegistrationCampSession.waitlist_updates` is a timestamped array of status changes on their
side). A flat `status` column loses that the moment #70 overwrites it. So:

- **`registration_status_events`** — append-only, one row per status transition.

  | Field               | Type                                         | Notes                                             |
  | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
  | `id`                | uuid                                         | primary key                                       |
  | `registration_id`   | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`               |                                                    |
  | `status`            | enum (`confirmed`, `waitlist`, `cancelled`)  |                                                    |
  | `changed_at`        | timestamp                                    | when the status actually changed, per Clubspot's own `waitlist_updates`/`confirmed_at` |
  | `recorded_at`       | timestamp, default now()                     | when #70's sync wrote this row (may lag `changed_at` if sync polls infrequently) |

  #70 should backfill this from Clubspot's own history (`waitlist_updates`, `confirmed_at`) rather
  than only logging transitions it happens to observe between polls — Clubspot already did the hard
  part. `registrations.status` stays as the current-value cache every other collection joins
  against; this table is where the history lives.

### Data provenance

People data is an aggregation, not a source: `people.email`/`phone` are collected from whatever a
registration's contact form said, and the same real person can supply different values on different
registrations (a guardian re-registers a second child two years later with a new email address).
Confirmed by looking at the actual participants spreadsheet (the thing #70/#95 replace): it's a
fully-rebuilt-every-run flat snapshot with **no timestamp or version on any row today** — there's
nothing to tell a conflicting value apart from a stale one, or to say which registration a person's
current email came from.

- **`person_field_history`** — append-only, one row per observed value.

  | Field                    | Type                                              | Notes                                  |
  | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
  | `id`                     | uuid                                              | primary key                            |
  | `person_id`              | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                          |                                         |
  | `field`                  | enum (`email`, `phone`, `first_name`, `last_name`) | which `people` field this observation is for |
  | `value`                  | string                                            |                                         |
  | `source_registration_id` | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`, nullable          | null if a staff member entered/corrected it directly in Directus instead |
  | `observed_at`            | timestamp                                        | the registration's own date — when this value was actually submitted |
  | `recorded_at`            | timestamp, default now()                          | when #70's sync wrote this row |

  `people.email`/`phone`/`first_name`/`last_name` stay as the current-value cache (#70 updates them
  to whichever source has the latest `observed_at`); this table is the audit trail behind them, and
  what a staff member would open to resolve "which of these two emails on file is right."

  Considered one polymorphic history table shared between this and `registration_status_events`
  (same shape: value + source + timestamps) — kept them separate instead. Two small, plainly-typed
  tables are easier to write permission filters against (e.g. a Guardian's own-minor scope) than one
  generic table needing a many-to-any relation to know what it's a history *of*.

### Auth identity

Auth info does not live on `people`. Directus already has its own identity table — `directus_users`
— with roles, policies, and OIDC `provider`/`external_identifier` fields for linking a Google login.
Reusing it instead of a homegrown field means:

- `people.directus_user_id` is a nullable, unique FK to `directus_users.id`. Set only for people who
  have an actual login: staff now (provisioned directly by an admin); coach/guardian later, once
  #65's account-linking flow provisions or links a `directus_users` row on first OIDC login.
- Directus's own OIDC config does the email-matching (`provider` + `external_identifier` on
  `directus_users`). This schema has no identity/matching logic of its own — it only points `people`
  at the resulting user once one exists.

### Permission model

- **Administrator** — Directus's built-in full-access role.
- **Staff** — authenticates via Directus's native Google OIDC, restricted to Workspace accounts an
  admin has provisioned as Directus users. Full read/write on every collection above, including
  `medical_profiles`. The only role delivered end-to-end by #69/#92-#95.
- **Coach** — defined now so the schema doesn't need reshaping later, but has no way to log in yet
  (needs #65). KISS for now: any authenticated Directus user can read `sessions` / `registrations` /
  `people` roster fields (no `medical_profiles`) — scoping a coach to only their own sessions via
  `event_staff` is a follow-up, not built here.
- **Guardian** — same login caveat as Coach. Policy: read their own minors' `people` /
  `medical_profiles` / `registrations`, filtered through `contacts` where
  `relationship_type == 'guardian'`. This scoping isn't KISS'd away like the coach roster case above
  — it's the medical-data boundary the whole design doc exists to get right.
- **Emergency contacts get no role or login.** They're informational rows staff can see on a minor's
  record (`contacts` where `relationship_type == 'emergency_contact'`), not a portal audience.

### Open questions for the applying slice (#95)

- Exact Directus field types (`uuid` vs. Directus's integer PKs) for every collection above — pick
  whichever keeps the permission filters simplest when building the real schema snapshot.
- Whether `medical_profiles` needs field-level (not just collection-level) permissions before a
  Guardian role ever actually logs in.
- The actual person-dedup rule #70 will use (email match, most likely, with a manual merge path for
  the rest) — out of scope here, but the schema above assumes one exists.

content.thinking:
This is a good question worth checking against what Directus already offers. I recall Directus has built-in activity and revision tracking that logs every create/update/delete with a JSON delta of changes and who made them, which could potentially replace the custom event/history tables I was planning.

Now I'm confirming the details: `directus_revisions` actually stores full snapshots of item state, not just deltas, linked to `directus_activity` for the event metadata — so this gives complete per-record versioning automatically, as long as changes go through the Directus API rather than raw SQL. The user's suggestion to lean on this instead of building bespoke tracking tables is a solid simplification that fits well with how the sync process is described.

Checking whether this actually covers registration status history: since every status update from the sync would go through the Directus API, each change generates a full-snapshot revision row timestamped and attributed to the sync's service account — meaning we could reconstruct status history by querying revisions filtered on collection and item ID, without needing a separate `registration_status_events` table. Though I'm noticing a subtlety around the exact timestamp semantics I'd want for `changed_at` that needs more thought.

Even if #70 replays each historical transition as a discrete write during a backfill, Directus would still stamp all those revisions with "when the backfill ran," not Clubspot's actual historical `changed_at` — so the revision log captures the sequence of states but not the true original timing.

That raises the real question of whether we even need Clubspot's true historical timestamp, or if "when we detected the change via sync" is good enough for what the user actually asked for.

Rereading the user's ask — they want visibility into the fact that changes happen over time, not necessarily perfect fidelity to Clubspot's own clock. Given their new question leans toward simplicity, I think the right call is to drop the bespoke tables and just rely on Directus's revision/activity log for both registration status and people field changes, while flagging that those timestamps reflect Directus's recording time rather than Clubspot's original event time.

I'm also considering provenance — Directus's activity log tracks which Directus user made a change, but since #70's sync likely runs under a single service account, that log won't distinguish which specific registration supplied a given value. So it covers "when" but not "which registration" for provenance purposes.

That could be a lightweight way to capture provenance—the sync leaving a comment like "updated email from registration #1234" whenever it changes a field, using Directus's own commenting feature instead of inventing a schema table for it.

So my answer to the user: Directus's built-in revisions/activity log already covers audit tracking for both registration status and contact field changes, meaning we can likely drop the bespoke history tables and rely on that instead, consistent with what architecture.md already anticipated. The main caveat is that this only captures writes made through the API, not raw SQL, so the sync process must go through the API for this to hold.

I also need to flag that Directus's revision timestamps reflect when Directus recorded the change, not necessarily the true historical moment from Clubspot's own timestamp data. If exact historical fidelity matters, a backfill importing Clubspot's status history would need to write each transition separately, but even then the revision timestamp would just reflect when the backfill ran—unless Directus's system fields like date_updated could somehow be overridden, which I don't think they can.

Separately, revisions attribute changes to the acting user, not to a specific source like which registration or session-join supplied the value. If that provenance matters, Directus's activity log alone won't capture it—we'd need either a sync comment noting the source, a dedicated source-pointer field, or a decision that this level of detail isn't actually necessary.

Given this trade-off, I should give a clear recommendation rather than punt the decision entirely: drop the separate history tables and lean on Directus's built-in revisions, but flag the source-attribution caveat explicitly so the user can weigh in on whether it matters to them.

My concrete proposal: drop `registration_status_events` and rely on Directus's built-in revisions/activity logs, since every status transition written through the API automatically becomes a revision. If exact historical timestamps matter more than sync-observed time, the backfill process could replay updates as sequential writes so the revision log preserves the correct order of state changes.

Similarly, I'd drop `person_field_history` and lean on the same revision log for `people` to track email/phone/name changes over time. But I'd keep a lightweight current `source_registration_id` pointer directly on `people` so staff can quickly see where the current contact info came from, letting Directus's revision history answer "how did this change" while the pointer answers "where did this come from" -- keeping things simple per the original "just snapshots" framing.

### Change tracking

Registration status isn't a fact that just happens once — a row moves waitlist → confirmed →
cancelled, and knowing _when_ matters (for reporting, and because Clubspot itself already tracks
it: `RegistrationCampSession.waitlist_updates` is a timestamped array of status changes on their
side). A flat `status` column loses that the moment #70 overwrites it. So:

- **`registration_status_events`** — append-only, one row per status transition.

  | Field             | Type                                        | Notes                                                                                  |
  | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `id`              | uuid                                        | primary key                                                                            |
  | `registration_id` | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`              |                                                                                        |
  | `status`          | enum (`confirmed`, `waitlist`, `cancelled`) |                                                                                        |
  | `changed_at`      | timestamp                                   | when the status actually changed, per Clubspot's own `waitlist_updates`/`confirmed_at` |
  | `recorded_at`     | timestamp, default now()                    | when #70's sync wrote this row (may lag `changed_at` if sync polls infrequently)       |

  #70 should backfill this from Clubspot's own history (`waitlist_updates`, `confirmed_at`) rather
  than only logging transitions it happens to observe between polls — Clubspot already did the hard
  part. `registrations.status` stays as the current-value cache every other collection joins
  against; this table is where the history lives.

### Data provenance

People data is an aggregation, not a source: `people.email`/`phone` are collected from whatever a
registration's contact form said, and the same real person can supply different values on different
registrations (a guardian re-registers a second child two years later with a new email address).
Confirmed by looking at the actual participants spreadsheet (the thing #70/#95 replace): it's a
fully-rebuilt-every-run flat snapshot with **no timestamp or version on any row today** — there's
nothing to tell a conflicting value apart from a stale one, or to say which registration a person's
current email came from.

- **`person_field_history`** — append-only, one row per observed value.

  | Field                    | Type                                               | Notes                                                                    |
  | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
  | `id`                     | uuid                                               | primary key                                                              |
  | `person_id`              | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                            |                                                                          |
  | `field`                  | enum (`email`, `phone`, `first_name`, `last_name`) | which `people` field this observation is for                             |
  | `value`                  | string                                             |                                                                          |
  | `source_registration_id` | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`, nullable           | null if a staff member entered/corrected it directly in Directus instead |
  | `observed_at`            | timestamp                                          | the registration's own date — when this value was actually submitted     |
  | `recorded_at`            | timestamp, default now()                           | when #70's sync wrote this row                                           |

  `people.email`/`phone`/`first_name`/`last_name` stay as the current-value cache (#70 updates them
  to whichever source has the latest `observed_at`); this table is the audit trail behind them, and
  what a staff member would open to resolve "which of these two emails on file is right."

  Considered one polymorphic history table shared between this and `registration_status_events`
  (same shape: value + source + timestamps) — kept them separate instead. Two small, plainly-typed
  tables are easier to write permission filters against (e.g. a Guardian's own-minor scope) than one
  generic table needing a many-to-any relation to know what it's a history _of_.

### Change tracking and provenance

Directus already does this: every API-driven create/update/delete is logged in `directus_activity`
(who, when, on what) with a paired `directus_revisions` row holding the full item snapshot and a
delta — for every collection, no opt-in needed. Architecture.md already assumed this
(`Audit — Directus activity log for data access/changes`), so there's no need for bespoke history
tables here, as long as #70 always writes through the Directus API (never raw SQL):

- **Registration status** (waitlist → confirmed → cancelled) doesn't need its own event log — the
  revision history on a `registrations` row already shows every state it's been in and when Directus
  recorded each change. If Clubspot's own historical timestamps
  (`RegistrationCampSession.waitlist_updates`) matter and not just "when we noticed," #70's first
  import of a registration can replay each transition as its own sequential write so the revision
  *order* matches reality — though the revision *timestamp* is always "when Directus saw the write,"
  not the original Clubspot moment; a backfill can't inject history at an arbitrary past time.
- **Person contact-field changes** (a guardian's email changing between registrations two years
  apart) are the same story: the revision history on a `people` row already shows every value
  `email`/`phone`/`first_name`/`last_name` has held. Confirmed by looking at the live participants
  spreadsheet (the thing #70/#95 replace) — it's a fully-rebuilt-every-run flat snapshot with no
  timestamp or version on any row today, which is the actual gap here, and Directus's activity log
  closes it without any schema of our own.

**What the activity log doesn't give us:** a revision is attributed to the Directus user who made
the write — for #70's automated updates that's always the sync's own service account, not *which
registration* supplied a given value. That's what `people.source_registration_id` (above) is for: a
plain current-value pointer, not a history table, answering "where did the email on file come from"
without needing to dig through revisions. If that turns out not to be worth the FK, it can go too —
"when this last changed" from the revision log may be enough on its own.

5	## People hub: schema and permission model
6	
7	Design doc for the Directus data model behind Layer 2 of `docs/architecture.md` (the CRM / people
8	hub), per the plan agreed on issue #69. Covers the collections, fields, and permission policies;
9	deployment and rollout are tracked in the sibling issues (#92-#95) that decompose #69.
10	
11	### Scope and non-goals
12	
13	- Models what Clubspot actually gives us: people, their guardian/emergency-contact relationships,
14	  programs/sessions/classes, and registrations. No household grouping — Clubspot has no concept of
15	  a household, only per-registration guardians and emergency contacts, so that's what the schema
16	  keys off.
17	- Terminology matches Clubspot and the website: **program** (Clubspot's `Camp`), **session**
18	  (`CampSession`), **class** (`CampClass`), **registration** (`Registration`/`RegistrationCampSession`)
19	  — not "enrollment."
20	- Registration status and person contact fields get **history, not just a current value** — see
21	  [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance).
22	- Auth identity is deliberately separate from person data — see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)
23	  below.
24	- Coach and guardian **portals** (thin clients calling this API) are out of scope; this doc defines
25	  the roles/policies they'll eventually use, but nothing here provisions their logins. That's #65.
26	
27	### Collections
28	
29	**people** — one row per human known to the org: staff, coaches, guardians, participants, emergency
30	contacts. Roles aren't stored — they're derived from relationships: staff from `directus_user_id` +
31	Directus role, coach from an `event_staff` row, guardian/emergency contact from a `contacts` row,
32	participant from a `registrations` row.
33	
34	No `clubspot_id` here. Clubspot has no stable person record — each registration carries its own
35	contact data, and one real person can show up as the contact on many registrations. Deduplicating
36	and collecting those into a single `people` row (by email, most likely) is the identity-resolution
37	problem #70's sync has to solve; it isn't a field this schema can just copy in.
38	
39	| Field                     | Type                                              | Notes                                                                                                                                  |
40	| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
41	| `id`                      | uuid                                              | primary key                                                                                                                            |
42	| `first_name`, `last_name` | string                                            |                                                                                                                                        |
43	| `email`, `phone`          | string, nullable                                  | contact info, not auth                                                                                                                 |
44	| `date_of_birth`           | date, nullable                                    | required for minors                                                                                                                    |
45	| `source_registration_id`  | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`, nullable          | which registration most recently supplied `email`/`phone`/name — see [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance) |
46	| `directus_user_id`        | uuid, nullable, unique, FK -> `directus_users.id` | see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)                                                                                                    |
47	
48	**medical_profiles** — one-to-one with `people`, kept as its own collection so its permission policy
49	can be stricter than a roster-level `people` read (allergies, medications, conditions, physician
50	contact).
51	
52	| Field                                    | Type                        | Notes                                             |
53	| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
54	| `person_id`                              | uuid, PK, FK -> `people.id` | one profile per person, so `person_id` is the key |
55	| `allergies`, `medications`, `conditions` | text                        | free-form                                         |
56	| `physician_name`, `physician_phone`      | string, nullable            |                                                   |
57	
58	**contacts** — one join collection for both relationship kinds Clubspot gives us (guardian and
59	emergency contact), rather than a separate table per type, since the shape is identical. Other
60	relationship kinds, if they're ever needed, get their own dedicated table rather than growing this
61	one's `relationship_type` enum.
62	
63	Like `people`, these rows have no Clubspot id of their own to key off — Clubspot doesn't model a
64	guardian/emergency contact as a linked record, just flat strings on the participant
65	(`parentGuardianName`/`_secondary`, `emergencyContact`/`emergencyRelationship`). `contact_order`
66	is what recovers Clubspot's primary-vs-secondary guardian distinction once #70 turns those flat
67	fields into rows here.

72	| `related_person_id` | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the minor                                 |
73	| `person_id`         | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the guardian or emergency contact         |
74	| `relationship_type` | enum (`guardian`, `emergency_contact`) |                                           |
75	| `contact_order`     | integer                                | call order when a minor has more than one |
76	
77	**event_staff** — coach/staff assigned to a session. This is the row that makes someone a "coach"
78	(derived, not stored on `people`) — not used to scope roster permissions yet, see
79	[Permission model](#permission-model).
80	
81	| Field        | Type                      | Notes       |
82	| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----------- |
83	| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
84	| `person_id`  | uuid, FK -> `people.id`   |             |

tags: [architecture, people-hub, directus]
---

## People hub: schema and permission model

Design doc for the Directus data model behind Layer 2 of `docs/architecture.md` (the CRM / people
hub), per the plan agreed on issue #69. Covers the collections, fields, and permission policies;
deployment and rollout are tracked in the sibling issues (#92-#95) that decompose #69.

### Scope and non-goals

- Models what Clubspot actually gives us: people, their guardian/emergency-contact relationships,
  programs/sessions/classes, and registrations. No household grouping — Clubspot has no concept of
  a household, only per-registration guardians and emergency contacts, so that's what the schema
  keys off.
- Terminology matches Clubspot and the website: **program** (Clubspot's `Camp`), **session**
  (`CampSession`), **class** (`CampClass`), **registration** (`Registration`/`RegistrationCampSession`)
  — not "enrollment."
- Registration status and person contact fields get **history, not just a current value** — see
  [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance).
- Auth identity is deliberately separate from person data — see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)
  below.
- Coach and guardian **portals** (thin clients calling this API) are out of scope; this doc defines
  the roles/policies they'll eventually use, but nothing here provisions their logins. That's #65.

### Collections

**people** — one row per human known to the org: staff, coaches, guardians, participants, emergency
contacts. Roles aren't stored — they're derived from relationships: staff from `directus_user_id` +
Directus role, coach from an `event_staff` row, guardian/emergency contact from a `contacts` row,
participant from a `registrations` row.

No `clubspot_id` here. Clubspot has no stable person record — each registration carries its own
contact data, and one real person can show up as the contact on many registrations. Deduplicating
and collecting those into a single `people` row (by email, most likely) is the identity-resolution
problem #70's sync has to solve; it isn't a field this schema can just copy in.

| Field                     | Type                                              | Notes                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                      | uuid                                              | primary key                                                                                                                            |
| `first_name`, `last_name` | string                                            |                                                                                                                                        |
| `email`, `phone`          | string, nullable                                  | contact info, not auth                                                                                                                 |
| `date_of_birth`           | date, nullable                                    | required for minors                                                                                                                    |
| `source_registration_id`  | uuid, FK -> `registrations.id`, nullable          | which registration most recently supplied `email`/`phone`/name — see [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance) |
| `directus_user_id`        | uuid, nullable, unique, FK -> `directus_users.id` | see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)                                                                                                    |

**medical_profiles** — one-to-one with `people`, kept as its own collection so its permission policy
can be stricter than a roster-level `people` read (allergies, medications, conditions, physician
contact).

| Field                                    | Type                        | Notes                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `person_id`                              | uuid, PK, FK -> `people.id` | one profile per person, so `person_id` is the key |
| `allergies`, `medications`, `conditions` | text                        | free-form                                         |
| `physician_name`, `physician_phone`      | string, nullable            |                                                   |

**contacts** — one join collection for both relationship kinds Clubspot gives us (guardian and
emergency contact), rather than a separate table per type, since the shape is identical. Other
relationship kinds, if they're ever needed, get their own dedicated table rather than growing this
one's `relationship_type` enum.

Like `people`, these rows have no Clubspot id of their own to key off — Clubspot doesn't model a
guardian/emergency contact as a linked record, just flat strings on the participant
(`parentGuardianName`/`_secondary`, `emergencyContact`/`emergencyRelationship`). `contact_order`
is what recovers Clubspot's primary-vs-secondary guardian distinction once #70 turns those flat
fields into rows here.

| Field               | Type                                   | Notes                                     |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `id`                | uuid                                   | primary key                               |
| `related_person_id` | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the minor                                 |
| `person_id`         | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the guardian or emergency contact         |
| `relationship_type` | enum (`guardian`, `emergency_contact`) |                                           |
| `contact_order`     | integer                                | call order when a minor has more than one |

**event_staff** — coach/staff assigned to a session. This is the row that makes someone a "coach"
(derived, not stored on `people`) — not used to scope roster permissions yet, see
[Permission model](#permission-model).

| Field        | Type                      | Notes       |
| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----------- |
| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
| `person_id`  | uuid, FK -> `people.id`   |             |
| `session_id` | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id` |             |

**programs** — matches org/Clubspot terminology: a program is what CYC calls a `Camp` in Clubspot
(e.g. "Youth Camp", "LTS Weekday", "ILCA Race Team") — the thing on the website you sign up for.

| Field              | Type                     | Notes                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `id`               | uuid                     | primary key                                                                    |
| `name`             | string                   |                                                                                |
| `category`         | string, nullable         | Clubspot's own grouping (e.g. "Summer Camp", "Junior Racing", "Adult Sailing") |
| `clubspot_camp_id` | string, nullable, unique | dedup key for #70                                                              |

**sessions** — a dated instance of a program (Clubspot's `CampSession`).

| Field                    | Type                      | Notes             |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `id`                     | uuid                      | primary key       |
| `program_id`             | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` |                   |
| `start_date`, `end_date` | date                      |                   |
| `clubspot_session_id`    | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70 |

**classes** — an age/skill subdivision within a program (Clubspot's `CampClass`, e.g. "Beginner" vs.
"Advanced"). Modeled now, not deferred: a registration is for a specific session _and_ class, and
#70's sync needs somewhere to put that — see `registrations` below.

| Field               | Type                      | Notes                                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                | uuid                      | primary key                                                            |
| `program_id`        | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` | a class belongs to the program, independent of which sessions offer it |
| `name`              | string                    |                                                                        |
| `clubspot_class_id` | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70                                                      |

Not modeled: which classes a given session offers (Clubspot's `CampSession.campClassesArray`) or
per-class/session capacity (`EntryCap`) — that's capacity-planning territory for the
financial-model-replacement app, not something the people hub's roster/permission needs require.

**registrations** — a participant's registration for one session + class (Clubspot's own term —
matched here rather than "enrollment"). This is deliberately at Clubspot's finest grain, its
`RegistrationCampSession` join ("Session Join Id" in the existing `ParticipantsReport`) rather than
its parent `Registration` object: a single Clubspot registration spanning multiple weeks/classes
becomes multiple rows here, one per session+class, matching what the current spreadsheet already
does. Billing/payment (Clubspot's `billing_registration`) stays out of scope, same as the rest of
the financial model.

| Field                      | Type                                        | Notes                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                       | uuid                                        | primary key                                                                                                                      |
| `person_id`                | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                     | the participant                                                                                                                  |
| `session_id`               | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id`                   |                                                                                                                                  |
| `class_id`                 | uuid, FK -> `classes.id`                    |                                                                                                                                  |
| `status`                   | enum (`confirmed`, `waitlist`, `cancelled`) | same vocabulary as #60; the _current_ status — see [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance) for history |
| `clubspot_registration_id` | string, nullable                            | groups rows from the same parent Clubspot registration (a multi-session signup); **not unique alone**                            |
| `clubspot_session_join_id` | string, nullable, unique                    | the true per-row dedup key for #70 (`RegistrationCampSession`'s own id)                                                          |

### Change tracking and provenance

Directus already does this: every API-driven create/update/delete is logged in `directus_activity`
(who, when, on what) with a paired `directus_revisions` row holding the full item snapshot and a
delta — for every collection, no opt-in needed. Architecture.md already assumed this
(`Audit — Directus activity log for data access/changes`), so there's no need for bespoke history
tables here, as long as #70 always writes through the Directus API (never raw SQL):

- **Registration status** (waitlist → confirmed → cancelled) doesn't need its own event log — the
  revision history on a `registrations` row already shows every state it's been in and when Directus
  recorded each change. If Clubspot's own historical timestamps
  (`RegistrationCampSession.waitlist_updates`) matter and not just "when we noticed," #70's first
  import of a registration can replay each transition as its own sequential write so the revision
  _order_ matches reality — though the revision _timestamp_ is always "when Directus saw the write,"
  not the original Clubspot moment; a backfill can't inject history at an arbitrary past time.
- **Person contact-field changes** (a guardian's email changing between registrations two years
  apart) are the same story: the revision history on a `people` row already shows every value
  `email`/`phone`/`first_name`/`last_name` has held. Confirmed by looking at the live participants
  spreadsheet (the thing #70/#95 replace) — it's a fully-rebuilt-every-run flat snapshot with no
  timestamp or version on any row today, which is the actual gap here, and Directus's activity log
  closes it without any schema of our own.

**What the activity log doesn't give us:** a revision is attributed to the Directus user who made
the write — for #70's automated updates that's always the sync's own service account, not _which
registration_ supplied a given value. That's what `people.source_registration_id` (above) is for: a
plain current-value pointer, not a history table, answering "where did the email on file come from"
without needing to dig through revisions. If that turns out not to be worth the FK, it can go too —
"when this last changed" from the revision log may be enough on its own.

### Auth identity

Auth info does not live on `people`. Directus already has its own identity table — `directus_users`
— with roles, policies, and OIDC `provider`/`external_identifier` fields for linking a Google login.
Reusing it instead of a homegrown field means:

- `people.directus_user_id` is a nullable, unique FK to `directus_users.id`. Set only for people who
  have an actual login: staff now (provisioned directly by an admin); coach/guardian later, once
  #65's account-linking flow provisions or links a `directus_users` row on first OIDC login.
- Directus's own OIDC config does the email-matching (`provider` + `external_identifier` on
  `directus_users`). This schema has no identity/matching logic of its own — it only points `people`
  at the resulting user once one exists.

### Permission model

- **Administrator** — Directus's built-in full-access role.
- **Staff** — authenticates via Directus's native Google OIDC, restricted to Workspace accounts an
  admin has provisioned as Directus users. Full read/write on every collection above, including
  `medical_profiles`. The only role delivered end-to-end by #69/#92-#95.
- **Coach** — defined now so the schema doesn't need reshaping later, but has no way to log in yet
  (needs #65). KISS for now: any authenticated Directus user can read `sessions` / `registrations` /
  `people` roster fields (no `medical_profiles`) — scoping a coach to only their own sessions via
  `event_staff` is a follow-up, not built here.
- **Guardian** — same login caveat as Coach. Policy: read their own minors' `people` /
  `medical_profiles` / `registrations`, filtered through `contacts` where
  `relationship_type == 'guardian'`. This scoping isn't KISS'd away like the coach roster case above
  — it's the medical-data boundary the whole design doc exists to get right.
- **Emergency contacts get no role or login.** They're informational rows staff can see on a minor's
  record (`contacts` where `relationship_type == 'emergency_contact'`), not a portal audience.

### Open questions for the applying slice (#95)

- Exact Directus field types (`uuid` vs. Directus's integer PKs) for every collection above — pick
  whichever keeps the permission filters simplest when building the real schema snapshot.
- Whether `medical_profiles` needs field-level (not just collection-level) permissions before a
  Guardian role ever actually logs in.
- The actual person-dedup rule #70 will use (email match, most likely, with a manual merge path for
  the rest) — out of scope here, but the schema above assumes one exists.
- Whether `medical_profiles` needs its own `source_registration_id`-style pointer — not built now (no
  evidence yet that medical data actually conflicts across registrations the way contact info can),
  but the pattern (a current-value pointer, history via Directus's own revision log) extends cleanly
  if it turns out to.
- `people.source_registration_id` and `registrations.person_id` are a circular FK pair. Not a
  problem in Postgres/Directus (both tables just need to exist before either constraint is added),
  but worth a heads-up so the migration/schema-apply order in #95 doesn't trip over it.

4	
5	## People hub: schema and permission model
6	
7	Design doc for the Directus data model behind Layer 2 of `docs/architecture.md` (the CRM / people
8	hub), per the plan agreed on issue #69. Covers the collections, fields, and permission policies;
9	deployment and rollout are tracked in the sibling issues (#92-#95) that decompose #69.
10	
11	### Scope and non-goals
12	
13	- Models what Clubspot actually gives us: people, their guardian/emergency-contact relationships,
14	  programs/sessions/classes, and registrations. No household grouping — Clubspot has no concept of
15	  a household, only per-registration guardians and emergency contacts, so that's what the schema
16	  keys off.
17	- Terminology matches Clubspot and the website: **program** (Clubspot's `Camp`), **session**
18	  (`CampSession`), **class** (`CampClass`), **registration** (`Registration`/`RegistrationCampSession`)
19	  — not "enrollment."
20	- Registration status and person contact fields get **history, not just a current value** — see
21	  [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance).
22	- Auth identity is deliberately separate from person data — see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)
23	  below.
24	- Coach and guardian **portals** (thin clients calling this API) are out of scope; this doc defines
25	  the roles/policies they'll eventually use, but nothing here provisions their logins. That's #65.
26	
27	### Collections
28	
29	**people** — one row per human known to the org: staff, coaches, guardians, participants, emergency
30	contacts. Roles aren't stored — they're derived from relationships: staff from `directus_user_id` +
31	Directus role, coach from an `event_staff` row, guardian/emergency contact from a `contacts` row,
32	participant from a `registrations` row.
33	
34	No `clubspot_id` here. Clubspot has no stable person record — each registration carries its own
35	contact data, and one real person can show up as the contact on many registrations. Deduplicating
36	and collecting those into a single `people` row (by email, most likely) is the identity-resolution
37	problem #70's sync has to solve; it isn't a field this schema can just copy in.
38	
39	| Field                     | Type                                              | Notes                               |
40	| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
41	| `id`                      | uuid                                              | primary key                         |
42	| `first_name`, `last_name` | string                                            |                                     |
43	| `email`, `phone`          | string, nullable                                  | contact info, not auth              |
44	| `date_of_birth`           | date, nullable                                    | required for minors                 |
45	| `directus_user_id`        | uuid, nullable, unique, FK -> `directus_users.id` | see [Auth identity](#auth-identity) |
46	
47	**medical_profiles** — one-to-one with `people`, kept as its own collection so its permission policy
48	can be stricter than a roster-level `people` read (allergies, medications, conditions, physician
49	contact).
50	
51	| Field                                    | Type                        | Notes                                             |
52	| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
53	| `person_id`                              | uuid, PK, FK -> `people.id` | one profile per person, so `person_id` is the key |
54	| `allergies`, `medications`, `conditions` | text                        | free-form                                         |
55	| `physician_name`, `physician_phone`      | string, nullable            |                                                   |
56	
57	**contacts** — one join collection for both relationship kinds Clubspot gives us (guardian and
58	emergency contact), rather than a separate table per type, since the shape is identical. Other
59	relationship kinds, if they're ever needed, get their own dedicated table rather than growing this
60	one's `relationship_type` enum.
61	
62	Like `people`, these rows have no Clubspot id of their own to key off — Clubspot doesn't model a
63	guardian/emergency contact as a linked record, just flat strings on the participant
64	(`parentGuardianName`/`_secondary`, `emergencyContact`/`emergencyRelationship`). `contact_order`
65	is what recovers Clubspot's primary-vs-secondary guardian distinction once #70 turns those flat
66	fields into rows here.
67	
68	| Field               | Type                                   | Notes                                     |
69	| ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
70	| `id`                | uuid                                   | primary key                               |
71	| `related_person_id` | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the minor                                 |
72	| `person_id`         | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the guardian or emergency contact         |
73	| `relationship_type` | enum (`guardian`, `emergency_contact`) |                                           |
74	| `contact_order`     | integer                                | call order when a minor has more than one |
75	
76	**event_staff** — coach/staff assigned to a session. This is the row that makes someone a "coach"
77	(derived, not stored on `people`) — not used to scope roster permissions yet, see
78	[Permission model](#permission-model).
79	
80	| Field        | Type                      | Notes       |
81	| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----------- |
82	| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
83	| `person_id`  | uuid, FK -> `people.id`   |             |
84	| `session_id` | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id` |             |
85	
86	**programs** — matches org/Clubspot terminology: a program is what CYC calls a `Camp` in Clubspot
87	(e.g. "Youth Camp", "LTS Weekday", "ILCA Race Team") — the thing on the website you sign up for.
88	
89	| Field              | Type                     | Notes                                                                          |
90	| ------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
91	| `id`               | uuid                     | primary key                                                                    |
92	| `name`             | string                   |                                                                                |
93	| `category`         | string, nullable         | Clubspot's own grouping (e.g. "Summer Camp", "Junior Racing", "Adult Sailing") |
94	| `clubspot_camp_id` | string, nullable, unique | dedup key for #70                                                              |
95	
96	**sessions** — a dated instance of a program (Clubspot's `CampSession`).
97	
98	| Field                    | Type                      | Notes             |
99	| ------------------------ | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
100	| `id`                     | uuid                      | primary key       |
101	| `program_id`             | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` |                   |
102	| `start_date`, `end_date` | date                      |                   |
103	| `clubspot_session_id`    | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70 |
104	
105	**classes** — an age/skill subdivision within a program (Clubspot's `CampClass`, e.g. "Beginner" vs.
106	"Advanced"). Modeled now, not deferred: a registration is for a specific session _and_ class, and
107	#70's sync needs somewhere to put that — see `registrations` below.
108	
109	| Field               | Type                      | Notes                                                                  |
110	| ------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |

Not modeled: which classes a given session offers (Clubspot's `CampSession.campClassesArray`) or
per-class/session capacity (`EntryCap`) — that's capacity-planning territory for the
financial-model-replacement app, not something the people hub's roster/permission needs require. No, please model this. This will be important both for financial modelling but also syncing the website - it's the darn schedule of the camp, and very important. I would rather capture more information during the initial use case of people sync than have to backfill a bunch of data later.

content.thinking:
I need to model how sessions relate to classes and capacity, since this schedule data matters for financial modeling and website sync, and they want it captured upfront rather than added later. A session can offer multiple classes and a class can span multiple sessions, so I'm thinking through whether to reuse an existing many-to-many structure or create a dedicated join for session-class offerings.

Looking closer, EntryCap already ties a class and session together, which is essentially the join table I need between sessions and classes — meaning capacity could live directly on that same relationship. I want to check the full EntryCap attributes to see if there's already a capacity number field defined alongside the class and session references.

content.thinking:
This confirms the model: an EntryCap ties a capacity number to a class and optionally a specific session, so an omitted session means the cap applies across all sessions for that class. I'm also noting that CampSession's class list determines which classes it offers, falling back to an "allClasses" flag when that list is empty.

So my schema needs a session_classes join table for explicit class listings, plus an all_classes boolean on sessions for the fallback case, and a separate capacity_limits/entry_caps table with class_id, nullable session_id, and cap integer to handle the scoped-versus-global capacity logic.

I should also add an `all_classes` boolean on sessions mirroring Clubspot's field, so a session can offer every class in the program without needing explicit `session_classes` rows.

For `entry_caps`, I'm mirroring Clubspot's EntryCap: id, class_id FK, nullable session_id FK, cap integer, and a nullable unique clubspot dedup id. This combination — classes, session_classes (or all_classes), and entry_caps — fully covers the camp schedule and capacity model, so registrations don't need any extra fields. Now I'll update the doc to replace the "not modeled" note with these concrete collections.

**sessions** — a dated instance of a program (Clubspot's `CampSession`).

| Field                    | Type                      | Notes                                                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `id`                     | uuid                      | primary key                                                                  |
| `program_id`             | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` |                                                                               |

| `all_classes`            | boolean                   | this session offers every class in the program, rather than a specific list (Clubspot's own `allClasses` flag) |
| `clubspot_session_id`    | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70                                                            |

**classes** — an age/skill subdivision within a program (Clubspot's `CampClass`, e.g. "Beginner" vs.
"Advanced"). A registration is for a specific session _and_ class — see `registrations` below.

| Field               | Type                      | Notes                                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                | uuid                      | primary key                                                            |
| `program_id`        | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` | a class belongs to the program, independent of which sessions offer it |
| `name`              | string                    |                                                                        |
| `clubspot_class_id` | string, nullable, unique  | dedup key for #70                                                      |

**session_classes** — which classes a session actually offers (Clubspot's
`CampSession.campClassesArray`), i.e. the camp schedule itself. A pure join, no fields of its own;
irrelevant for a session where `sessions.all_classes` is true (every program class applies). No
Clubspot id of its own — it's an array on `CampSession`, not a separate object — so #70 just
reconciles it to match Clubspot's array each sync (remove rows no longer present, add new ones).

| Field        | Type                      | Notes |
| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----- |
| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
| `session_id` | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id` |       |
| `class_id`   | uuid, FK -> `classes.id`  |       |

**entry_caps** — capacity, matching Clubspot's `EntryCap` exactly: a cap on one class, either
overall (`session_id` null, applies across every session) or for one specific session.

| Field                  | Type                                     | Notes                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                   | uuid                                     | primary key                                 |
| `class_id`             | uuid, FK -> `classes.id`                 |                                              |
| `session_id`           | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id`, nullable      | null = applies to this class across all sessions |
| `cap`                  | integer                                  | the actual limit (Clubspot's own field name) |
| `clubspot_entry_cap_id` | string, nullable, unique                | dedup key for #70                           |

This — `programs` / `sessions` / `classes` / `session_classes` / `entry_caps` — is the camp
schedule: worth capturing accurately from #70's first sync rather than backfilling later, since the
website and the eventual financial-model app both need it, not just rosters/permissions.

5	## People hub: schema and permission model
6	
7	Design doc for the Directus data model behind Layer 2 of `docs/architecture.md` (the CRM / people
8	hub), per the plan agreed on issue #69. Covers the collections, fields, and permission policies;
9	deployment and rollout are tracked in the sibling issues (#92-#95) that decompose #69.
10	
11	### Scope and non-goals
12	
13	- Models what Clubspot actually gives us: people, their guardian/emergency-contact relationships,
14	  the camp schedule (programs/sessions/classes/capacity), and registrations. No household
15	  grouping — Clubspot has no concept of a household, only per-registration guardians and emergency
16	  contacts, so that's what the schema keys off.
17	- Terminology matches Clubspot and the website: **program** (Clubspot's `Camp`), **session**
18	  (`CampSession`), **class** (`CampClass`), **registration** (`Registration`/`RegistrationCampSession`)
19	  — not "enrollment."
20	- Registration status and person contact fields get **history, not just a current value** — see
21	  [Change tracking and provenance](#change-tracking-and-provenance).
22	- Auth identity is deliberately separate from person data — see [Auth identity](#auth-identity)
23	  below.
24	- Coach and guardian **portals** (thin clients calling this API) are out of scope; this doc defines
25	  the roles/policies they'll eventually use, but nothing here provisions their logins. That's #65.
26	
27	### Collections
28	
29	**people** — one row per human known to the org: staff, coaches, guardians, participants, emergency
30	contacts. Roles aren't stored — they're derived from relationships: staff from `directus_user_id` +
31	Directus role, coach from an `event_staff` row, guardian/emergency contact from a `contacts` row,
32	participant from a `registrations` row.
33	
34	No `clubspot_id` here. Clubspot has no stable person record — each registration carries its own
35	contact data, and one real person can show up as the contact on many registrations. Deduplicating
36	and collecting those into a single `people` row (by email, most likely) is the identity-resolution
37	problem #70's sync has to solve; it isn't a field this schema can just copy in.
38	
39	| Field                     | Type                                              | Notes                               |
40	| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
41	| `id`                      | uuid                                              | primary key                         |
42	| `first_name`, `last_name` | string                                            |                                     |
43	| `email`, `phone`          | string, nullable                                  | contact info, not auth              |
44	| `date_of_birth`           | date, nullable                                    | required for minors                 |
45	| `directus_user_id`        | uuid, nullable, unique, FK -> `directus_users.id` | see [Auth identity](#auth-identity) |
46	
47	**medical_profiles** — one-to-one with `people`, kept as its own collection so its permission policy
48	can be stricter than a roster-level `people` read (allergies, medications, conditions, physician
49	contact).
50	
51	| Field                                    | Type                        | Notes                                             |
52	| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
53	| `person_id`                              | uuid, PK, FK -> `people.id` | one profile per person, so `person_id` is the key |
54	| `allergies`, `medications`, `conditions` | text                        | free-form                                         |
55	| `physician_name`, `physician_phone`      | string, nullable            |                                                   |
56	
57	**contacts** — one join collection for both relationship kinds Clubspot gives us (guardian and
58	emergency contact), rather than a separate table per type, since the shape is identical. Other
59	relationship kinds, if they're ever needed, get their own dedicated table rather than growing this
60	one's `relationship_type` enum.
61	
62	Like `people`, these rows have no Clubspot id of their own to key off — Clubspot doesn't model a
63	guardian/emergency contact as a linked record, just flat strings on the participant
64	(`parentGuardianName`/`_secondary`, `emergencyContact`/`emergencyRelationship`). `contact_order`
65	is what recovers Clubspot's primary-vs-secondary guardian distinction once #70 turns those flat
66	fields into rows here.
67	
68	| Field               | Type                                   | Notes                                     |
69	| ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
70	| `id`                | uuid                                   | primary key                               |
71	| `related_person_id` | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the minor                                 |
72	| `person_id`         | uuid, FK -> `people.id`                | the guardian or emergency contact         |
73	| `relationship_type` | enum (`guardian`, `emergency_contact`) |                                           |
74	| `contact_order`     | integer                                | call order when a minor has more than one |
75	
76	**event_staff** — coach/staff assigned to a session. This is the row that makes someone a "coach"
77	(derived, not stored on `people`) — not used to scope roster permissions yet, see
78	[Permission model](#permission-model).
79	
80	| Field        | Type                      | Notes       |
81	| ------------ | ------------------------- | ----------- |
82	| `id`         | uuid                      | primary key |
83	| `person_id`  | uuid, FK -> `people.id`   |             |
84	| `session_id` | uuid, FK -> `sessions.id` |             |
85	
86	**programs** — matches org/Clubspot terminology: a program is what CYC calls a `Camp` in Clubspot
87	(e.g. "Youth Camp", "LTS Weekday", "ILCA Race Team") — the thing on the website you sign up for.
88	
89	| Field              | Type                     | Notes                                                                          |
90	| ------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
91	| `id`               | uuid                     | primary key                                                                    |
92	| `name`             | string                   |                                                                                |
93	| `category`         | string, nullable         | Clubspot's own grouping (e.g. "Summer Camp", "Junior Racing", "Adult Sailing") |
94	| `clubspot_camp_id` | string, nullable, unique | dedup key for #70                                                              |
95	
96	**sessions** — a dated instance of a program (Clubspot's `CampSession`).
97	
98	| Field                    | Type                      | Notes                                                                                                          |
99	| ------------------------ | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
100	| `id`                     | uuid                      | primary key                                                                                                    |
101	| `program_id`             | uuid, FK -> `programs.id` |                                                                                                                |
102	| `start_date`, `end_date` | date                      |                                                                                                                |
